s0: A language model can recommend a trade in seconds. The hard part is trusting it with money. AlphaAgent puts three models in an argument, then hands the answer to code that cannot be talked round. No prompt can move money here; only the guard, which knows nothing about language models.
s1: Here is the interface. A request to buy forty-five shares of NVDA at a hundred dollars arrives at the portfolio. The guard approves ten point four nine units instead - one thousand forty-nine dollars, eighteen cents. Five percent of cash. Every limit is visible in the same header: exposure, concentration, per-trade size and the daily loss cap.
s2: Three agents argued first. A bull analyst built the case to buy. A risk assessor built the case to sell, and neither saw the other's prompt. The chief investment officer weighed both and named the objection it could not answer. Nothing about their disagreement is summarised away.
s3: The deliberation is on screen, not summarised away. Claims, evidence and the rebuttal that answered them, each tagged with its source and horizon. Positive coverage on the left, negative on the right, and the decision quality underneath.
s4: And every request is checked against limits the model cannot see. A second request after a six hundred dollar loss is refused, because the daily limit is five hundred. The arithmetic is printed next to the refusal. The refusal names the rule, the amount and the limit it breached.
s5: Run the decision again and you get the same answer, from a replay bundle you can open in a browser with no database and no key. Open source, on GitHub.
